docs.title: gpuprov
docs.text:
GPU machines with Kubernetes on them, from one command. gpuprov provisions a GPU VM on the cheapest cloud offer that has capacity, turns it into a single-node k3s cluster, waits until both SSH and the cluster are healthy, and records the result locally. You can then use it over plain SSH or deploy containers with kubectl.

$ gpuprov provision --name dev --gpus L4:1 --cloud gcp --region us-central1 --region us-east1
VM 'dev' is UP
  Endpoint:    ubuntu@34.122.x.x:22
  Connect:     gpuprov ssh dev    (or plain: ssh dev)

Kubernetes cluster 'gpuprov-dev' is ready.
  API:         https://34.122.x.x:6443
  Kubeconfig:  ~/.gpu-provisioner/kube/dev.yaml

$ gpuprov ssh dev -- nvidia-smi
$ KUBECONFIG=~/.gpu-provisioner/kube/dev.yaml kubectl get nodes
$ gpuprov down dev

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Multi-cloud, one interface. AWS, GCP, budget GPU clouds (Massed Compute, Hyperstack, Lambda, Verda), GPU marketplaces (Prime Intellect, RunPod), and a local Docker "cloud" for tests all sit behind one CloudProvider trait of six idempotent primitives.
  • Failover that does not leak. Offers are tried in price order. A capacity error tears down the partial attempt and moves on, and a quota error skips the whole region. If teardown cannot be confirmed, the VM is recorded as LEAKED instead of being forgotten.
  • Durable state machines. Every operation is journaled in local SQLite. Ctrl-C cleans up what the run created, and a crash resumes from the last state. It never creates a second instance, because every step observes the cloud before it acts. See State machines.
  • Kubernetes by default. On clouds with cloud-init, k3s installs while the VM boots. gpuprov then verifies that install over SSH and falls back to pushing the installer itself when needed. GPU nodes get the NVIDIA runtime and device plugin, and every cluster is validated before you get a kubeconfig. Opt out with --no-k8s.
  • SSH-native. One local ed25519 key and a per-VM ~/.ssh/config entry, so plain ssh dev, VS Code Remote, and rsync work.
  • No server. A single binary with state in ~/.gpu-provisioner.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From crates.ioFrom source 
cargo install gpu-provisioner      # installs the `gpuprov` binary

git clone https://github.com/DumbAI/gpu-provisioner
cd gpu-provisioner
cargo install --path .

Requirements: Rust 1.91.1 or newer, and the system OpenSSH client (ssh) on your PATH. On macOS and Linux it is already there.

docs.title: Try it without a cloud account
docs.text:
The docker cloud runs each "VM" as a local sshd container. It's the quickest way to see the whole lifecycle. Containers can't run k3s, so these come up as plain VMs:

gpuprov provision --cloud docker --name demo --instance-type container
gpuprov ssh demo -- uname -a
gpuprov status demo        # the journaled state transitions
gpuprov down demo

docs.title: Your first cloud VM
docs.text:
1. Credentials. Use whatever each cloud's own tooling already uses. Details are in Configuration.

    • AWS: aws configure (or a profile in ~/.gpu-provisioner/config.toml).
    • GCP: gcloud auth login and gcloud config set project <id>.
    • Prime Intellect: prime login, or PRIME_API_KEY.
    • RunPod: RUNPOD_API_KEY (or runpod config).
    • Verda: VERDA_CLIENT_ID and VERDA_CLIENT_SECRET (Cloud API credentials).
    • Massed Compute, Hyperstack, Lambda: MASSED_COMPUTE_API_KEY, HYPERSTACK_API_KEY, LAMBDA_API_KEY.

  2. Provision.

    # AWS: the cheapest T4 type in us-west-2, falling back to us-east-1
gpuprov provision --name dev --gpus T4:1 --region us-west-2 --region us-east-1

# GCP: an L4 in any zone of us-central1
gpuprov provision --cloud gcp --name dev-gcp --gpus L4:1 --region us-central1

# Budget 48 GB GPU for a session: Massed Compute (US) or Hyperstack (Canada)
gpuprov provision --cloud massedcompute --name dev-mc --gpus A6000:1
gpuprov provision --cloud hyperstack --name dev-hs --gpus A6000:1 --region CANADA-1

# RunPod: the cheapest in-stock RTX 4090 pod (pods run as containers: no k3s)
gpuprov provision --cloud runpod --name dev-rp --gpus RTX4090:1

# Prime Intellect: the cheapest H100 offer anywhere in the marketplace
gpuprov provision --cloud primeintellect --name dev-pi --gpus H100:1

    Each VM is also a single-node k3s cluster by default. The command blocks until SSH works and the cluster is validated, then prints the kubeconfig path. Add --no-k8s for a plain VM. Progress goes to stderr and the summary to stdout.

  3. Use it.

    gpuprov ssh dev                    # interactive shell
gpuprov ssh dev -- nvidia-smi      # one command; the exit code propagates
ssh dev                            # plain OpenSSH works too
gpuprov list

  4. Tear it down. VMs bill until you do.

    gpuprov down dev

docs.title: When things go wrong
docs.text:
• Ctrl-C during provision finishes the in-flight cloud call, then deletes what this run created. Press it twice to exit immediately. Re-running the same command then resumes from the journal.
  • gpuprov status <name> shows the last operation and its recent transitions, including why each failed offer was skipped.
  • A VM shown as LEAKED means teardown could not be confirmed. Run gpuprov down <name> again, or gpuprov provision with the same name, which cleans up first.

docs.title: Adding a cloud
docs.text:
A cloud is one module under src/provider/<id>/ that implements CloudProvider, plus one line in provider::build. Nothing above the trait changes. Failover, retries, polling, deadlines, compensation, crash recovery, the journal, SSH, and k3s all come from the shared core.

#[async_trait]
pub trait CloudProvider: Send + Sync {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;                 // "mycloud": recorded on every VM row
    fn capabilities(&self) -> Capabilities;         // unsupported features + timing hints
    async fn plan(&self, req: &ResourceRequest) -> Result<Vec<Offer>, ProviderError>;
    async fn prepare(&self, offer: &Offer, spec: &InstanceSpec) -> Result<serde_json::Value, ProviderError>;
    async fn create(&self, offer: &Offer, prepared: &serde_json::Value, spec: &InstanceSpec) -> Result<String, ProviderError>;
    async fn observe(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str) -> Result<Vec<Observed>, ProviderError>;
    async fn delete(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str, ids: &[String]) -> Result<(), ProviderError>;
    async fn cleanup(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str) -> Result<(), ProviderError>;
}

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
Primitive Must Must not plan return offers in preference order (cheapest first). Put anything create needs (marketplace ids, sockets) into Offer::detail. create anything prepare be idempotent per (VM, location): firewall/security group, key registration, image resolution. Return private JSON; it is journaled. create the instance create make one attempt and label everything with the VM identity (tag, label, or name gpuprov-<vm>) wait for running, or retry observe return all non-terminated instances with that identity, with normalized InstanceStatus, and the SshEndpoint once reachable (user/port if the cloud dictates them) filter out broken instances (report them as Failed) delete request deletion; unknown or already-gone ids count as success wait cleanup delete per-VM side resources; idempotent touch shared resources (keys, VPCs)

Long waits belong to the core, which polls observe using your Capabilities { boot_timeout, delete_timeout, poll_interval }. The one exception is a bounded wait on a cloud operation whose result carries the error, as with GCP's operations.wait after instances.insert.

docs.title: Classifying errors
docs.text:
Map every API failure to an ErrorKind. This is the entire failover policy, and it lives in your error.rs:

Kind Use for Core does Transient throttling, 5xx, timeouts retries the step with backoff. Creating observes first, so a request that actually landed is adopted, not duplicated. Capacity stockouts tears down, blocks the offer, and moves to the next Quota account limits tears down and blocks the whole region (override with with_block) Unavailable not viable here and nothing was created blocks the offer with no teardown Failed anything else after resources may exist tears down, blocks the offer, and moves to the next InvalidRequest the ask can't be satisfied (unknown GPU, bad zone) aborts Credentials auth failures tears down what may exist, then aborts

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. src/provider/<id>/mod.rs, with pub const PROVIDER_ID, the provider struct, and the trait impl. The module doc should map each primitive to the cloud API calls it makes.
  2. A config section in config.rs, and an arm in AppConfig::default_regions if your region names differ from AWS's.
  3. Register it in provider::build and PROVIDER_IDS.
  4. Tests: pure tests for parsing and classification, plus wiremock tests for every HTTP primitive. Add a test-only constructor that takes a base URL so tests never read env or credential files. See provider/primeintellect and provider/gcp.
  5. A page under docs/clouds/, and a row in the comparison table.

docs.title: Provisioning State Machines — Design
docs.text: Status: implemented. This page describes the code in src/machine/, src/vm/, src/cluster/, and src/provider/. Section 1 records the review of the previous design that motivated it. Scope: the VM lifecycle state machine (launch, teardown), the k3s cluster state machine layered on it, and the provider contract that every cloud adapter implements (AWS, GCP, Massed Compute, Hyperstack, Lambda, Verda, Prime Intellect, RunPod, and the Docker test cloud).

docs.title: 1. Review of the previous design
docs.text:
The previous pipeline (orchestrator.rs → failover.rs → CloudProvider) was a readable plan → provision-with-failover → wait-for-SSH sequence with a sound error taxonomy. Its weaknesses showed up as soon as a second, differently-shaped cloud (Prime Intellect) was attempted:

# Problem Where Consequence 1 The state machine is implicit. The DB stored PROVISIONING/UP/FAILED/TERMINATED; the real stages (plan, bootstrap, create, wait-running, wait-ssh, persist, k3s) existed only as control flow. orchestrator::launch, failover::provision_with_failover A crash or Ctrl-C mid-launch lost the failover cursor and any created instance id. Recovery depended on name-tag find-or-create in the one region still on the row. 2 Leak paths. TeardownFailed marked the row FAILED and moved on. FAILED/PROVISIONING rows were never reconciled. A fatal error (e.g. credentials) after create aborted with no teardown. failover.rs, orchestrator.rs:76 Billing resources could outlive every record pointing at them. 3 Coarse, loop-heavy provider trait. provision = bootstrap + find-or-create; wait_running polled for up to 10 minutes inside the adapter, and the engine retried it 3× (up to 30 min). Retry/backoff/polling was re-implemented per adapter. provider/aws/instance.rs:34, failover.rs:24 Every new cloud re-wrote the robustness logic, which is where bugs hide. 4 AWS-shaped assumptions above the trait. The SSH endpoint was public_ip:22 with a client-chosen user; the key travelled by cloud-init; ports, AMI and spot were assumed. orchestrator::finalize, ssh/config_file.rs Marketplace clouds (Prime Intellect: provider-chosen user and NAT port, keys registered via API, no firewall API) did not fit. 5 Blocklist scope fixed at (type, region). failover.rs:139 Quota errors (region-wide) retried every type. Marketplace offers (one per data center) were over-blocked. 6 k3s lived in main.rs, outside any state. finalize_kubernetes ran after the VM was marked UP. The installer travelled by cloud-init and readiness was kubectl get nodes on the node. main.rs:194, kube.rs A failed k3s install left an UP VM with no record of it. k3s only worked on clouds with cloud-init and inbound ports. A closed port 6443 was not caught.

docs.title: 2. Goals
docs.text:
1. One shared, failure-tolerant core. Retries, backoff, polling, deadlines, cancellation, crash-resume and compensation (teardown) are written once.
  2. Thin, uniform cloud adapters. An adapter exposes small, idempotent primitives and classifies its errors; it contains no loops or sleeps beyond a single API call's own pagination.
  3. No silent leaks. Every state that may own a cloud resource knows where it is. A failed teardown is a persistent Leaked state that the next command must resolve.
  4. Composable machines. The k3s machine embeds the VM machine as a child and adds its own durable steps.
  5. Stay true to the PRD wedge: a single binary with local SQLite state and no server.

docs.title: 3. Alternatives considered
docs.text: Decision Options Choice and rationale Execution model (a) implicit control flow (status quo) · (b) edge-triggered workflow of explicit persisted states · (c) level-triggered reconciler (Kubernetes-controller style: desired vs observed, loop until converged) · (d) external durable-execution engine (Temporal) (b) with (c) inside each step. Failover is an ordered search with a cursor, which is naturally a workflow. But each step is written as observe → act if needed → observe (e.g. Creating first looks for an existing instance before calling create), so re-running any step after a crash is safe. (d) violates the single-binary constraint. State encoding Rust typestate · hand-rolled enum + step() · FSM crate (statig, rust-fsm) enum + step(). Typestate cannot be serialized and resumed after a crash. A crate adds a dependency but still needs custom persistence. Serde enums give persistence for free. Provider granularity Coarse (provision, wait) · fine primitives (plan / prepare / create / observe / delete / cleanup) Fine primitives. Coarse calls let an adapter optimise, but they duplicate polling and retry and hide progress from the journal. Fine primitives move all waiting into the core. Passing offer details from plan to launch Encode in the instance-type string (e.g. provider__gpu__cpu__mem) · adapter-side cache · opaque detail JSON on the Offer, persisted Persisted JSON survives crashes, keeps the core cloud-agnostic, and avoids string parsing. Transient-error retries Per adapter · central (core) One retry policy and one budget. Adapters return ErrorKind::Transient. SDK-internal retries for reads stay, since they are cheap and safe. k3s installer delivery cloud-init at boot only · SSH push after Ready only · boot first, verified over SSH, SSH push as fallback Boot delivery overlaps the install with the SSH wait (about 1–2 minutes faster) but is unobservable and exists only on cloud-init clouds. SSH push works everywhere and is retryable, but is serial. The hybrid gets both: CheckingBootInstall reads the installer's status marker and pushes over SSH only when the boot route is missing (no cloud-init, reused VM), failed, or ran too long. A host-wide lock and an idempotent installer make the two routes safe to overlap. k3s by default opt-in --k8s · on by default, opt out with --no-k8s / [defaults] kubernetes = false Every VM is a ready cluster. The default is skipped, with a note, on clouds that cannot host k3s (Feature::Kubernetes unsupported, e.g. Docker); an explicit --k8s there is rejected up front. k3s API access Always public :6443 · Direct when the cloud can open ports, else SshTunnel Makes k3s portable to clouds without a firewall API. Validation checks the access path the user will actually use. Projection vs source of truth One table · machines (journal, source of truth) + vms (user-facing projection) The generic executor must not know VM columns. vms is updated idempotently by steps and can always be recomputed.

docs.title: 4. Architecture
docs.text:
main.rs ─ CLI: provision / down / status / ssh / kubeconfig / tunnel / list
  cluster/k3s.rs      K3sMachine     = Vm(child LaunchMachine) → Install → ApiReady → Kubeconfig → Validate
  vm/launch.rs        LaunchMachine  = Reconcile → Plan → [Prepare → Create → Boot → Connect]* → Ready
  vm/teardown.rs      TeardownMachine= Request → AwaitGone → Cleanup → Done   (also the compensation sub-machine)
    machine/          Executor<M: Machine>: persist · retry budget · backoff · poll · deadline · cancel · resume
                      Journal (SQLite `machines` + `machine_events`)
      provider/mod.rs CloudProvider: capabilities · plan · prepare · create · observe · delete · cleanup
        provider/{aws, gcp, massedcompute, hyperstack, lambda, verda, primeintellect, runpod, docker}/   — the only code that talks to a cloud API

docs.title: 4.1 The provider contract (provider/mod.rs)
docs.text:
#[async_trait]
pub trait CloudProvider: Send + Sync {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn capabilities(&self) -> Capabilities;                       // unsupported features, boot timeout, poll interval
    async fn plan(&self, req: &ResourceRequest) -> Result<Vec<Offer>, ProviderError>;
    async fn prepare(&self, offer: &Offer, spec: &InstanceSpec) -> Result<serde_json::Value, ProviderError>;
    async fn create(&self, offer: &Offer, prepared: &serde_json::Value, spec: &InstanceSpec)
        -> Result<String /* instance id */, ProviderError>;
    async fn observe(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str) -> Result<Vec<Observed>, ProviderError>;
    async fn delete(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str, instance_ids: &[String]) -> Result<(), ProviderError>;
    async fn cleanup(&self, at: &Location, vm_name: &str) -> Result<(), ProviderError>;
}

Semantics every adapter must honour. These are checked by the shared conformance tests and the fake-provider tests.

Primitive Contract plan Ordered offers (preference = order). Pure catalog/availability lookup that creates nothing. Unplannable ask → InvalidRequest. prepare Idempotent per-(VM, location) prerequisites (security group, firewall rule, SSH-key registration, image resolution). Returns driver-private JSON, persisted. create One creation attempt. Every resource is labelled with the VM identity (gpuprov-vm-name=<name> tag or label, or the gpuprov-<name> name). No waiting for running. observe All non-terminated instances carrying the identity at that location, with normalised status and the SSH endpoint once known. delete Request deletion of the given instances. Idempotent: an unknown or already-deleted instance is success. Does not wait. cleanup Delete per-VM side resources after instances are gone. Idempotent.

Normalised status: Pending | Running | Stopping | Stopped | Terminating | Failed(reason). The core treats an instance as booted when it is Running and reports an SshEndpoint { host, port, user? }. That covers the AWS public-IP lag and Prime Intellect's late sshConnection.

ProviderError { kind, msg, block } drives the core:

ErrorKind Core action Default block scope Transient retry the same step with backoff (budgeted) — Capacity compensate → block → next offer the offer Quota compensate → block → next offer the whole region (all types) Unavailable block → next offer, no compensation (nothing created) the offer Failed compensate → block → next offer the offer InvalidRequest, Credentials compensate if something may exist → Aborted —

An adapter may override the scope through block (for example AWS Unsupported → instance type in region).

docs.title: 4.2 The executor (machine/)
docs.text:
#[async_trait]
pub trait Machine: Send + Sync {
    type State: Serialize + DeserializeOwned + Clone + Debug + Send + Sync;
    const KIND: &'static str;
    fn is_terminal(&self, s: &Self::State) -> bool;
    fn label(&self, s: &Self::State) -> String;                       // journal / progress line
    async fn step(&self, s: &Self::State, cx: &StepCx) -> Step<Self::State>;
    fn retry_policy(&self, s: &Self::State) -> RetryPolicy { RetryPolicy::default() }
    fn on_retries_exhausted(&self, s: &Self::State, last_error: String) -> Self::State;
    fn on_cancel(&self, s: &Self::State) -> Option<Self::State> { None }
}

pub enum Step<S> {
    Next(S),                                   // transition, persisted before the next step runs
    Poll { after: Duration, note: String },   // not done yet: same state, no budget consumed
    Retry { error: String },                  // transient: same state, backoff, budget consumed
}

Executor invariants:

  1. Write-ahead. A transition is journalled before the next step's side effect. Steps that produce a handle (for example Creating → Booting { instance_id }) return it in the next state, so it is durable before any wait begins.
  2. Idempotent steps. Because a crash can happen after a side effect but before its transition is journalled, each step tolerates re-execution (observe first).
  3. Budgets. Consecutive Retrys in one state are capped (RetryPolicy { max_attempts, initial_backoff, max_backoff }). On exhaustion the machine names the failure state; the executor never invents one. Poll deadlines are enforced by the machine using cx.in_state (time since entering the state in this process), so a resume gets a fresh but bounded window.
  4. Cancellation at step boundaries only. Ctrl-C never drops an in-flight cloud call (that would lose the handle). Between steps, on_cancel maps the state to a compensating state (for example Booting → Compensating). The machine then runs to a terminal state, and a second Ctrl-C exits immediately and leaves the journal resumable.
  5. Resume. Executor::run loads the journalled state for the key. If it is non-terminal, execution continues from it; otherwise the caller supplies a fresh initial state.

docs.title: 4.3 VM launch machine (vm/launch.rs)
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Reconciling
    Reconciling --> Connecting: UP record & cloud says Running (reuse)
    Reconciling --> Compensating: journal shows Leaked / stale attempt
    Reconciling --> Planning
    Planning --> Preparing: offers (cursor = 0)
    Planning --> Aborted: InvalidRequest / Credentials
    Preparing --> Creating
    Creating --> Booting: instance id (or adopted existing)
    Booting --> Connecting: Running + SSH endpoint
    Connecting --> Ready: SSH login OK, ssh config + vms row written
    Preparing --> NextOffer: Unavailable (no compensation)
    Creating --> Compensating: Capacity / Quota / Failed
    Booting --> Compensating: Failed status / boot timeout / vanished
    Connecting --> Compensating: SSH timeout
    Compensating --> NextOffer: teardown complete → block scope
    Compensating --> Leaked: teardown exhausted
    NextOffer --> Preparing: next unblocked offer
    NextOffer --> Exhausted: none left
    Exhausted --> Planning: --retry-until-up (after 30 s)
    Ready --> [*]
    Aborted --> [*]
    Leaked --> [*]

Search { offers, cursor, blocked, history } travels in every attempt state, so the failover cursor survives a crash. Leaked { location, instance_ids, reason } is terminal for this run, but the next provision or down for the name starts by compensating it, and list/status show it.

docs.title: 4.4 Teardown machine (vm/teardown.rs)
docs.text: Requesting → AwaitingGone → CleaningUp → Done | Leaked. It is used standalone by down and embedded by the launch machine's Compensating state, so one teardown implementation serves both paths.

docs.title: 4.5 k3s cluster machine (cluster/k3s.rs)
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Vm
    Vm --> CheckingBootInstall: child LaunchMachine Ready
    Vm --> Failed: child Exhausted / Aborted / Leaked
    CheckingBootInstall --> CheckingBootInstall: boot install running (poll, ≤ 15 min)
    CheckingBootInstall --> AwaitingApi: installed at boot
    CheckingBootInstall --> Installing: not installed / failed / timed out / GPU missed
    Installing --> AwaitingApi: installer pushed over SSH (idempotent)
    AwaitingApi --> FetchingKubeconfig: /readyz ok
    FetchingKubeconfig --> Validating: kubeconfig written (Direct or SshTunnel)
    Validating --> Validating: API cert lacks public host → re-run installer with SAN (once)
    Validating --> Ready: node Ready, CoreDNS up, GPU allocatable, cert SAN ok, API reachable
    Installing --> Failed: retries exhausted
    AwaitingApi --> Failed: timeout
    Validating --> Failed: timeout
    Ready --> [*]
    Failed --> [*]
  • Boot first, SSH as fallback. On clouds whose capabilities report boot_script, K3sMachine::new sets the installer as the VM's InstanceSpec::boot_script, a structured script plus env, so k3s installs while the VM boots. Each adapter delivers it natively: AWS and GCP render it into cloud-init (userdata::render), and Verda creates a startup-script resource (BootScript::to_shell). The k3s layer never touches a cloud-specific format. The installer serializes on a host-wide flock, records state=running|done|failed in /var/lib/gpuprov/k3s-install.status, and owns /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml (re-rendered from a SAN list, restarting k3s only when it changes). CheckingBootInstall reads the marker plus cloud-init status, the k3s unit state, and GPU presence in one SSH round trip. A pure decision table (kube::BootProbe::decide) maps that to installed, wait, or fall back to SSH.
  • TLS SAN. At boot the installer learns the public IP from the AWS/GCP metadata services. If that fails, Validating sees the API certificate doesn't cover the public host and re-runs the installer once with the SAN.
  • Composition. K3sState::Vm(LaunchState) delegates step to the child machine and lifts its result. A child terminal Ready(vm) becomes CheckingBootInstall { vm }. One journal row per VM name holds the whole nested state.
  • Access mode. Direct (the cloud opens 6443/80/443) or SshTunnel (gpuprov tunnel <name> forwards 127.0.0.1:6443). The choice comes from provider capabilities, so k3s works on Prime Intellect.
  • Failure policy. k3s failures leave the VM up (Failed { vm }) for debugging. gpuprov down removes it, and re-running gpuprov provision reuses the VM and re-enters at CheckingBootInstall.

docs.title: 6. Testing
docs.text:
• Executor tests: a toy machine checks persistence, resume after a simulated crash, retry exhaustion, and the cancellation mapping.
  • Launch-machine tests: a scripted FakeProvider covers failover across offers, quota blocking a region, crash between create and journal (adopts the instance and does not create a duplicate), fatal error after create (compensates), and a failed teardown (Leaked, resolved by the next run).
  • Adapter tests: pure classification and parsing tests. HTTP adapters (every cloud except AWS and Docker) run against wiremock.
  • Integration (tests/docker_e2e.rs, #[ignore] unless Docker is present): the docker provider provisions a real sshd container through the full launch machine, runs a command over SSH, re-provisions idempotently, and tears down. Run with cargo test --test docker_e2e -- --ignored.

docs.title: Clouds
docs.text: Every cloud is an adapter behind the same six-primitive CloudProvider contract. The shared state machines supply failover, retries, compensation, and crash recovery; each adapter only maps a cloud's API onto the contract. Pick one with --cloud <id>.

docs.title: Pick a cloud
docs.text:
For… Use cheap 24–48 GB NVIDIA GPUs for a development session massedcompute (US), hyperstack (Canada) a second, independent US source when one is sold out lambda the hyperscalers you already have accounts with aws, gcp European capacity, spot pricing verda marketplace breadth (many upstream providers) primeintellect, runpod trying gpuprov without any account docker

Prices and stock change minute to minute. Every adapter except AWS and GCP plans from live availability, so the offers are what can actually be launched now, cheapest first.

docs.title: Support status
docs.text: Adapters are tested against each cloud's documented API, with pure tests plus mock HTTP servers. A cloud is labeled supported only after a real-account run of the acceptance suite: allocate, SSH, k3s + GPU, terminate, verify nothing billable remains, and interrupt-midway cleanup. See that page for the current results.

docs.title: AWS
docs.text: gpuprov provision --name dev --gpus A10G:1 --region us-east-2 --region us-west-2

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
A GPU ask maps to a ladder of EC2 types, cheapest first: same GPU, more CPU and RAM as you go up. The ladder is crossed type-major with your regions, so the cheapest type is tried in every region before a bigger one.

GPU count → types T4 1 → g4dn.xlarge … g4dn.16xlarge · 4 → g4dn.12xlarge · 8 → g4dn.metal A10G 1 → g5.xlarge … g5.16xlarge · 4 → g5.12xlarge, g5.24xlarge · 8 → g5.48xlarge L4 1 → g6.xlarge … g6.16xlarge · 4 → g6.12xlarge, g6.24xlarge · 8 → g6.48xlarge L40S 1 → g6e.xlarge … g6e.16xlarge · 4 → g6e.12xlarge, g6e.24xlarge · 8 → g6e.48xlarge A100 · A100-80GB · H100 · H200 8 → p4d.24xlarge · p4de.24xlarge · p5.48xlarge · p5e.48xlarge

docs.title: Prepare (per offer)
docs.text:
Checks run cheapest first, so a region that isn't viable fails before anything is created:

  1. Instance-type metadata (GPU, architecture) and the zones that actually offer the type.
  2. AMI: the Ubuntu / Deep Learning AMI matching GPU and architecture, resolved through SSM public parameters (or --image). Its root device and minimum disk size are validated.
  3. Public subnets in the default VPC, restricted to the offering zones.
  4. A per-VM security group (gpuprov-<name>) opening 22 plus requested ports.

Default AMIs, keyed on the instance type's live metadata:

x86_64 arm64 CPU Canonical Ubuntu 22.04 Canonical Ubuntu 22.04 (arm64) GPU Deep Learning Base AMI (OSS NVIDIA driver) Deep Learning Base AMI arm64 (OSS NVIDIA driver)

Pre-Turing GPUs (K80/V100/M60) are not supported by the OSS driver; pass --image for those. A --disk smaller than the AMI's snapshot is rejected with the required size.

docs.title: Create / observe / delete
docs.text:
• RunInstances uses a no-retry client and walks the zones' subnets on capacity errors. Instances use IMDSv2 and gp3 root disks, and are tagged gpuprov-vm-name=<name> and gpuprov-managed=true. The SSH key travels in cloud-init; no EC2 key pairs are created.
  • observe uses DescribeInstances filtered by the identity tag. delete is TerminateInstances (a not-found instance counts as success). cleanup deletes the security group, retrying while ENIs detach.

docs.title: Error mapping
docs.text: AWS code Kind Effect InsufficientInstanceCapacity, InsufficientCapacity, … Capacity compensate, next offer VcpuLimitExceeded, InstanceLimitExceeded, MaxSpotInstanceCountExceeded Quota skip the whole region Unsupported Unavailable skip this type in the region RequestLimitExceeded, InternalError, … Transient retry with backoff AuthFailure, ExpiredToken, … Credentials abort (after compensating)

docs.title: IAM permissions
docs.text: The caller needs ec2:Describe*, ec2:RunInstances, ec2:TerminateInstances, ec2:CreateTags, ec2:CreateSecurityGroup, ec2:DeleteSecurityGroup, ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress, and ssm:GetParameter (public AMI parameters). The VM itself gets no IAM role.

docs.title: Docker (local test cloud)
docs.text:
The docker cloud runs each "VM" as a long-running sshd container on your local Docker daemon. It exists so the real state machines (journaling, failover bookkeeping, SSH probing, reuse, crash adoption, teardown) can run end to end without a cloud account. CI uses it the same way.

gpuprov provision --cloud docker --name demo --instance-type container
gpuprov ssh demo -- 'whoami && sudo -n true && echo ok'
gpuprov down demo
Primitive Docker plan one offer in region local (GPU asks are rejected) prepare check the daemon; build the embedded sshd image on first use (its tag includes the Dockerfile hash) create docker run -d, labeled gpuprov-vm-name=<name>, SSH published on 127.0.0.1:<random port> observe docker ps -a by label, plus docker inspect for status and mapped port delete docker rm -f

The container's entrypoint gives the same login contract that cloud-init gives a real VM: $SSH_USER with passwordless sudo and the public key authorized.

Containers don't run systemd, so --k8s cannot install k3s here. Use this cloud for VM-lifecycle testing.

docs.title: GCP
docs.text:
gcloud auth login && gcloud config set project my-project
gpuprov provision --cloud gcp --name dev --gpus L4:1 --region us-central1 --region us-east1

The adapter calls the Compute Engine v1 REST API directly. Authentication uses an OAuth access token from [gcp] access_token, $GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN, or gcloud auth print-access-token (cached and refreshed). Leaving out service-account key signing keeps the binary free of crypto dependencies.

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
GCP capacity is zonal, so offers are per zone. The GPU ladder below is crossed with the zones of each region, but only zones that actually offer the machine type (live aggregated/machineTypes / aggregated/acceleratorTypes) are kept.

GPU count → machine types T4 1 → n1-standard-4/8/16 · 2 → n1-standard-8/16 · 4 → n1-standard-16/32 (T4 attached as a guest accelerator) L4 1 → g2-standard-4 … g2-standard-32 · 2 → g2-standard-24 · 4 → g2-standard-48 · 8 → g2-standard-96 A100 1/2/4/8 → a2-highgpu-{1,2,4,8}g A100-80GB 1/2/4/8 → a2-ultragpu-{1,2,4,8}g H100 1/2/4/8 → a3-highgpu-{1,2,4,8}g

docs.title: Prepare / create
docs.text:
• prepare makes sure a per-VM firewall rule gpuprov-<name> exists, allowing tcp:22 plus requested ports to the instance's network tag. It also resolves the image: the Deep Learning VM family common-cu129-ubuntu-2204-nvidia-580 for GPU types (CUDA 12.9, driver 580), and ubuntu-2204-lts otherwise, unless you pass --image.
  • create runs instances.insert with labels gpuprov-vm-name/gpuprov-managed, ssh-keys and cloud-init user-data metadata, a public NAT IP, and onHostMaintenance=TERMINATE for GPUs. --spot gives a SPOT instance that is deleted on preemption. It then waits for the zone operation, a bounded wait, because stockouts only show up in the finished operation.

docs.text: Operation / HTTP error Kind Effect ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED(_WITH_DETAILS), UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION, RESOURCE_NOT_READY Capacity next zone QUOTA_EXCEEDED (incl. GPUS_ALL_REGIONS) Quota skip the region VPC_NOT_FOUND Unavailable skip the region 429 / 5xx / network Transient retry 401, non-quota 403 Credentials abort

docs.title: Hyperstack
docs.text:
Hyperstack rents GPU virtual machines by the hour in three regions: CANADA-1 (Quebec), US-1 (Texas) and NORWAY-1. For small workloads, Canada is the useful one, with inexpensive single-GPU flavors such as RTX A6000 48 GB, L40 48 GB and RTX PRO 6000 96 GB. Texas mostly offers eight-GPU H100/A100 configurations.

export HYPERSTACK_API_KEY=...          # or [hyperstack] api_key in config.toml
gpuprov provision --cloud hyperstack --name dev --gpus A6000:1
gpuprov provision --cloud hyperstack --name big --gpus L40:1 --region CANADA-1
gpuprov provision --cloud hyperstack --name eu --gpus A6000:1 --region NORWAY-1

Acceptance testing pending

The adapter is built and tested against Hyperstack's published API (official OpenAPI spec), but it has not yet passed a live acceptance run: fresh account → API key → one GPU → SSH → k3s/GPU readiness → terminate → no billable resources left, plus an interrupted provision. Treat it as preview until that run is recorded.

docs.title: Planning: flavor ⨝ stock ⨝ price
docs.text:
An offer is emitted only when three live sources agree:

  1. Flavor (GET /core/flavors): the configuration exists in the region and reports stock_available.
  2. Stock (GET /core/stocks): when the region lists the GPU model, it must have a free configuration of that GPU count (1x, 2x, 4x, 8x).
  3. Price (GET /pricebook): the per-GPU hourly rate × GPU count. Spot GPUs are priced under <gpu>-spot.

Each surviving flavor × region is one offer, cheapest first:

  • instance_type = the flavor name, e.g. n3-RTX-A6000x1
  • region = CANADA-1, US-1 or NORWAY-1

Default regions are the North American ones (CANADA-1, US-1). Norway is only searched when you ask for it with --region NORWAY-1, so a Norway-only flavor never appears in a North American plan.

--gpus A6000:1 matches the RTX-A6000 GPU on whole name tokens (A100-80GB matches A100-80G-PCIe; L40 does not match L40S). --instance-type takes an exact flavor name. --spot switches to the spot flavor family (flavors with spot in their name).

Stock is re-checked for the chosen flavor right before deploying, so a stale offer fails without creating anything. A deploy that hits a stock-out moves on to the next offer.

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
Resource Notes VM named gpuprov-<name>, labeled gpuprov-vm-name=<name> and gpuprov-managed, with a public IP firewall rules inbound TCP 22 plus requested ports, set in the create call environment gpuprov-<region> (e.g. gpuprov-canada-1), created once per region and shared by gpuprov VMs there key pair your gpuprov public key, imported once per environment and reused

The image is the newest Ubuntu with the newest CUDA for GPU flavors (the variant without Docker on a tie; k3s brings its own runtime), plain Ubuntu for CPU flavors, or whatever the flavor is hard-restricted to. --image takes any Hyperstack image name. You log in as ubuntu on port 22: gpuprov disables the API's port randomization when it assigns the public IP.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: Hyperstack VMs boot with cloud-init, so the k3s installer rides in the VM's user data and k3s installs while the VM boots. gpuprov then verifies the install over SSH. Firewall rules are part of the create call, so the API (6443) and ingress (80/443) are opened and clusters use direct access.

docs.title: Teardown
docs.text: gpuprov down deletes the VM (a VM that is already gone counts as deleted). Its public IP goes with it. The shared environment and key pair stay for the next VM in that region; delete them in the Hyperstack console if you want them gone.

docs.title: Open questions for the acceptance run
docs.text:
• Whether inline security_rules at create time are applied as documented, or whether rules must be added after creation (POST …/sg-rules).
  • That enable_port_randomization: false keeps SSH on port 22 of the public IP.
  • The exact pricebook names for spot GPUs (<gpu>-spot per the billing docs).

docs.title: Lambda
docs.text:
Lambda rents on-demand GPU instances (full VMs) in several US regions, billed per minute. Instances boot the Lambda Stack image (Ubuntu with NVIDIA drivers, CUDA and common ML frameworks).

export LAMBDA_API_KEY=...          # or [lambda] api_key in config.toml
gpuprov provision --cloud lambda --name dev --gpus A6000:1
gpuprov provision --cloud lambda --name big --gpus H100:8 --region us-east-1

Create an API key at https://cloud.lambda.ai/api-keys.

Acceptance testing pending

This adapter is covered by unit and mock-API tests. It has not yet passed the end-to-end acceptance run against a live account (allocate → SSH → k3s/GPU ready → terminate → nothing billable left), so treat it as preview.

docs.title: Planning: live capacity
docs.text:
One call, GET /api/v1/instance-types, returns every instance type with its price and the regions that can launch it right now. Each type × region with capacity becomes one offer:

  • instance_type = Lambda's type, e.g. gpu_1x_a6000 or gpu_8x_h100_sxm5
  • region = Lambda region (us-east-1, us-west-1, …); there are no zones
  • ordered by hourly price, cheapest first

Without --region, only US regions (us-*) are considered. Pass --region explicitly for any other region. --zone also pins a region, because Lambda has no zones.

--gpus matches the GPU description by whole tokens: A10 does not match A100, A6000 matches the RTX A6000, A100-80GB matches only the 80 GB A100, and H100:1 picks the single-GPU PCIe type while H100:8 picks the 8× SXM5 box. --instance-type takes an exact type name, including CPU types.

Capacity is re-checked right before launching, so a stale offer fails before anything is registered or created.

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
Resource Notes instance named and hostnamed gpuprov-<name>, tagged gpuprov-vm-name=<name> and gpuprov-managed=true firewall ruleset only when extra ports are needed (--port, or the k3s API); named gpuprov-<name>, allows SSH plus those ports, deleted on teardown SSH key your gpuprov public key, registered once and reused; never removed

The login user is ubuntu, created by gpuprov's cloud-init user data. --image takes a Lambda image family (e.g. lambda-stack-24-04) or an image id.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: Launches accept cloud-init user data, so the k3s installer runs while the VM boots and gpuprov verifies it over SSH. Firewall rulesets attach per instance, so clusters use direct API access: ports 6443, 80 and 443 are opened in the VM's ruleset.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Feature Why --spot Lambda offers on-demand instances only

Lambda's legacy account-wide firewall rules do not apply in us-south-1, and gpuprov uses per-instance rulesets instead. If a region rejects ruleset creation, that offer is skipped and the next one is tried.

docs.title: Teardown
docs.text: gpuprov down terminates the instance, waits until Lambda reports it gone, then deletes the VM's firewall ruleset in that region. While the instance is still terminating the ruleset is "in use", so the delete is retried until it frees up.

docs.title: Massed Compute
docs.text:
Massed Compute rents full GPU VMs by the hour from its US data centers, with a strong low-cost range of 24–48 GB cards (RTX A5000, RTX A6000, L40S) and A100s. It's a good default for "a usable GPU development machine for a few dollars per session."

export MASSED_COMPUTE_API_KEY=...     # or [massedcompute] api_key
gpuprov provision --cloud massedcompute --name dev --gpus A6000:1
gpuprov provision --cloud massedcompute --name big --gpus A100-80GB:1
gpuprov ssh dev -- nvidia-smi

Create the token under Settings → API at vm.massedcompute.com/settings/api with Full access. A read-only token can plan but not launch.

docs.title: Planning: live inventory
docs.text:
gpuprov reads the current inventory (GET /api/v1/gpu-inventory). Every product with capacity becomes one offer:

  • instance_type = the product, e.g. gpu_1x_a6000 (1× RTX A6000)
  • region = any, because the launch API doesn't let you choose a data center and Massed Compute places the VM
  • ordered by hourly price, cheapest first

--gpus A6000:2 picks products with exactly two RTX A6000s. GPU names match on whole tokens, so L40 does not match L40S and A10 does not match A100. --instance-type takes an exact product name, CPU products included.

--region keeps only products that currently have capacity in one of the named regions (e.g. us-central-3), but cannot pin placement. Massed Compute's data centers are all in the US, so there is no default region filter.

Capacity is re-checked right before launching, so a stale offer fails without creating anything.

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
Resource Notes instance named gpuprov-<name>; matched by that name SSH key your gpuprov public key, registered once under gpuprov-<hash> and reused (any existing entry with the same key is reused as-is); never removed

The image defaults to the newest plain Ubuntu image from GET /api/v1/images. Desktop and app-specific stacks are skipped. --image takes an image id or an exact image name.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text: You log in on port 22 as the user the instance reports, which is Ubuntu on the Ubuntu images (capital U). gpuprov records it, so gpuprov ssh <name> and plain ssh <name> just work.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Instances are full VMs, so the default k3s cluster works. The installer is pushed over SSH after the VM is up. The API has a startup command, but its run-as user, size limit, and whether it runs on every boot aren't documented, so gpuprov doesn't rely on it.

There is no firewall API, so clusters use SSH-tunnel access (gpuprov tunnel <name>).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Rejected up front:

Feature Why --port no firewall API: ports other than SSH cannot be opened or guaranteed reachable --spot only on-demand instances are offered

Things to know:

  • Stopped VMs keep billing. gpuprov only ever terminates.
  • A low account balance ("Insufficient Funds") ends a launch immediately with a clear message.
  • The running-instance cap tied to your billing Recharge Amount is reported as a quota error. Raise the recharge amount on the Billing page.
  • Disk size (--disk) is fixed by the product; the API has no disk option.

Acceptance testing pending

This adapter follows the published VM API reference. It hasn't yet been run end to end against a real account (allocate → SSH → k3s/GPU ready → terminate → no billable resources left, plus an interrupted launch).

docs.title: Prime Intellect
docs.text:
Prime Intellect is a GPU marketplace. It resells capacity from upstream providers (Hyperstack, Lambda, DataCrunch, Nebius, …) behind one API, which makes it a natural fit for failover across providers.

export PRIME_API_KEY=...          # or `prime login`, or [primeintellect] api_key
gpuprov provision --cloud primeintellect --name dev --gpus H100:1
gpuprov provision --cloud primeintellect --name dev2 --gpus A100:8 --region united_states

docs.title: Planning: live availability
docs.text:
gpuprov queries GET /api/v1/availability/gpus live instead of shipping a static catalog. A marketplace's stock changes minute to minute, so a static catalog would be stale on arrival. Each in-stock offer becomes one candidate:

  • instance_type = <provider>/<cloudId> (e.g. hyperstack/n3-H100x1)
  • region = a Prime Intellect region id (united_states, canada, eu_west, …). No --region means anywhere.
  • zone = the data center id, which --zone pins
  • ordered by on-demand price, cheapest first

GPU names match on a boundary: H100 matches H100_80GB, A100 matches both A100 sizes, H200 does not match GH200, and A10 does not match A100. --instance-type accepts <provider>/<cloudId> or a bare cloudId.

docs.title: Prepare / create
docs.text:
• prepare looks up or registers our public key under /ssh_keys and passes its id per pod (sshKeyId), leaving the account's primary key alone. It then re-checks stock for that exact offer, so a stale plan fails before anything is created.
  • create posts /pods using the offer's own socket (SXM offers need the right value; a fixed PCIe would be wrong for them), data center, security tier, and image. Pods are named gpuprov-<name>.

docs.title: SSH and Kubernetes
docs.text: The SSH user and port come from the pod's sshConnection (often root and a NAT port), not from --ssh-user. Pods expose SSH only, so --port is rejected, and --k8s clusters use SSH-tunnel access.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: These are declared as unsupported features and rejected up front: --port (no firewall API), --image (images come from the offer's environment list), and --spot. Pods can take up to about 16 minutes to become active, so the boot budget is 16 minutes.

docs.title: RunPod
docs.text:
RunPod rents GPUs by the hour from its own data centers (secure cloud) and from vetted hosts (community cloud). A RunPod "VM" is a pod: a GPU container, reached over SSH as root.

export RUNPOD_API_KEY=...          # or [runpod] api_key, or ~/.runpod/config.toml
gpuprov provision --cloud runpod --name dev --gpus RTX4090:1
gpuprov provision --cloud runpod --name big --gpus H100:8 --region north_america
gpuprov ssh dev -- nvidia-smi

docs.title: Planning: live availability
docs.text:
gpuprov asks RunPod's catalog for current stock (GET /v2/catalog/gpus?include=AVAILABILITY&product=POD) once per cloud tier, and turns every data center that has the GPU in stock into one offer:

  • instance_type = <RunPod GPU id> x<count> <tier>, e.g. NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 x1 community
  • region = the data center's continent (north_america, europe, asia, …)
  • zone = the data center id (US-TX-3, EU-RO-1, …), which --zone pins
  • ordered by hourly price (secure and community tiers compete), cheapest first

--region accepts continents or ISO country codes (--region US --region CA). No --region means anywhere.

GPU names match on whole tokens: H100 matches every H100 variant (PCIe, SXM, NVL), A100-80GB matches both 80 GB A100s, RTX4090 matches the GeForce RTX 4090, and L40 does not match L40S. --instance-type takes an exact RunPod GPU id, such as "NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3".

Because stock changes minute to minute, prepare re-checks the chosen data center right before creating, so a stale offer fails without creating anything.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Pods are created with port 22/tcp published and the public key passed in the PUBLIC_KEY environment variable. Official runpod/* images start sshd from it. gpuprov adds the keys already registered on your account, read-only, so your own SSH keys keep working. Your account's key list is never modified.

SSH goes to the pod's ssh.direct endpoint, a public IP plus a random port mapped to 22, as root. gpuprov ssh <name> and plain ssh <name> handle the port for you.

docs.title: Images
docs.text: The default image is runpod/base:1.4.1-cuda1290-ubuntu2204 (Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.9). Override it per VM with --image or for all pods with [runpod] image. A custom image must start sshd from $PUBLIC_KEY; images built on the official runpod/* images do.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
These are rejected up front:

Feature Why --port pod ports are published on random public ports, not the requested number --spot the REST API has no interruptible pods --k8s pods are containers without systemd, so k3s cannot run; the default k3s cluster is skipped with a note

Pods can take several minutes to pull a large image, so the boot budget is 15 minutes. Disk (--disk) is the pod's container disk, which is wiped if the pod restarts.

docs.title: Verda
docs.text:
Verda is a GPU cloud with dedicated GPU and CPU instances (real VMs) in European data centers. Instances are billed hourly, either on demand or as spot capacity.

export VERDA_CLIENT_ID=... VERDA_CLIENT_SECRET=...   # or [verda] in config.toml
gpuprov provision --cloud verda --name dev --gpus H100:1
gpuprov provision --cloud verda --name cheap --gpus A100:1 --spot --region FI

Credentials are the Cloud API credentials (client ID and secret) from the Verda console's Credentials page. gpuprov exchanges them for a short-lived OAuth token and refreshes it automatically.

docs.title: Planning: live availability
docs.text:
gpuprov reads the instance-type catalog and the current per-location availability (GET /v1/instance-availability, spot or on-demand to match --spot). Each location that has the type in stock becomes one offer:

  • instance_type = Verda's type, e.g. 1H100.80S.22V (1× H100 SXM5, 22 vCPUs)
  • region = the location code (FIN-01, FIN-02, ICE-01, …)
  • ordered by hourly price (the spot price with --spot), cheapest first

--region accepts location codes or ISO country codes (--region FI). No --region means anywhere. --gpus H100:8 picks types with exactly eight H100s; --instance-type takes an exact type, including CPU-only types.

Stock is re-checked for the chosen location right before deploying, so a stale offer fails without creating anything. A deploy that hits "no capacity" moves on to the next offer.

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
Resource Notes instance tagged gpuprov-vm-name=<name> and gpuprov-managed=true; hostname gpuprov-<name> OS volume --disk GB, tagged the same; deleted permanently with the instance startup script the k3s installer (see below), one per VM, removed on teardown SSH key your gpuprov public key, registered once and reused; never removed

The image is picked from the instance type's supported OS list: the newest Ubuntu with CUDA for GPU types, plain Ubuntu for CPU types. --image takes any Verda image type. You log in as root.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Verda runs a startup script as root on first boot, so the k3s installer goes in as a startup script and k3s installs while the VM boots. gpuprov then verifies the install over SSH and falls back to pushing the installer itself if needed.

Verda has no firewall API, so gpuprov cannot guarantee that ports other than SSH are reachable. Clusters therefore use SSH-tunnel access (gpuprov tunnel <name>), and --port is rejected.

docs.title: Teardown
docs.text: gpuprov down deletes the instance together with its volumes (permanently, not to the trash). It then sweeps any volume still tagged for the VM, plus the VM's startup scripts. Teardown is retried until Verda confirms the instance is gone; otherwise the VM is recorded as LEAKED.

docs.title: Provider acceptance
docs.text: Unit and mock-server tests prove that an adapter speaks a cloud's API as documented. They cannot prove that the cloud actually allocates, boots, and cleans up reliably for a real account. Before a provider is labeled supported, run the acceptance suite (tests/acceptance.rs) against it with a fresh account.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Test Steps full_lifecycle allocate one VM for the ask → SSH login → nvidia-smi -L lists a GPU (GPU asks) → k3s installed and validated, GPU allocatable (where the cloud supports k3s) → terminate → the cloud reports no instances left and per-VM cleanup is idempotent interrupted_provision_cleans_up start a launch, "press Ctrl-C" once the instance is booting → the launch compensates and ends cancelled → nothing is left

Each run uses a fresh temporary GPUPROV_HOME and a unique VM name, and prints the journaled timeline (seconds since start for every transition). A drop guard tears the VM down if a test fails midway, so a failed run doesn't keep billing.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
The suite creates billable resources, so it is #[ignore]d and also needs GPUPROV_ACCEPT=1:

GPUPROV_ACCEPT=1 \
GPUPROV_ACCEPT_CLOUD=hyperstack \
GPUPROV_ACCEPT_GPUS=A6000:1 \
GPUPROV_ACCEPT_REGIONS=CANADA-1 \
  cargo test --test acceptance -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1
Variable Meaning GPUPROV_ACCEPT_CLOUD provider id (required) GPUPROV_ACCEPT_GPUS or GPUPROV_ACCEPT_INSTANCE_TYPE the ask (exactly one) GPUPROV_ACCEPT_REGIONS comma-separated regions (else the cloud's default) GPUPROV_ACCEPT_K8S 0 to skip the k3s stage GPUPROV_ACCEPT_CONFIG config file with credentials (else ~/.gpu-provisioner/config.toml, else env vars)

Use the cheapest single-GPU offer the cloud has. The suite's value is in the lifecycle, not the hardware.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: gpuprov ships as the gpu-provisioner crate on crates.io; it provides the gpuprov binary and the gpu_provisioner library.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Bump version in Cargo.toml (semver).
  2. Make sure CI is green, and run the e2e suite locally if Docker-touching code changed.

  3. Check what will be uploaded. Cargo.toml include limits the package to src/, tests/, examples/*.yaml, Cargo.lock, the README, and the LICENSE. The docs site and design notes stay out.

    cargo package --list
cargo publish --dry-run

  4. Publish (irreversible: a version can be yanked but never re-used or deleted):

    cargo login            # token from https://crates.io/me
cargo publish
git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0

docs.title: Docs site
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme from docs/:

uv run --with-requirements docs/requirements.txt mkdocs serve        # http://127.0.0.1:8000
uv run --with-requirements docs/requirements.txt mkdocs build --strict
uv run --with-requirements docs/requirements.txt mkdocs gh-deploy    # publish to GitHub Pages

(Use pip install -r docs/requirements.txt in place of uv if you prefer.)

The live site is https://dumbai.github.io/gpu-provisioner/, served by GitHub Pages from the gh-pages branch. .github/workflows/docs.yml builds the site strictly on pull requests and redeploys it on every push to main that touches docs/ or mkdocs.yml, so mkdocs gh-deploy by hand is only needed out of band.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
cargo test                       # all unit tests: no cloud or Docker needed
cargo test vm::launch            # one module (substring match)
cargo test quota_blocks_every_type_in_the_region   # one test
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --check
cargo test --test vendor_stubs   # every cloud adapter against a stateful stub of its API
cargo test --test docker_e2e -- --ignored --nocapture   # end-to-end, needs Docker

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Layer How it's tested Executor (machine/) a toy machine: journaling, retry-budget exhaustion, resume from a journaled state, cancel → compensation, cancel → resumable Launch / teardown / k3s machines provider::fake::FakeProvider, a small simulated cloud with scripted per-offer behaviors (Boots, CreateFails, CreatedButErrors, BootFails, NeverBoots, …), injectable delete failures, a call log, and a max-concurrent-instances counter for leak and duplicate checks Adapters pure parsing and classification tests, plus wiremock HTTP servers for each HTTP cloud Adapters + state machines vendor API stubs: stateful simulations of each vendor's API (moto for AWS), five shared scenarios per vendor End to end tests/docker_e2e.rs: the Docker cloud plus real SSH. It provisions, runs a command, re-provisions (reuse), simulates a crash after create (adopts the container, no duplicate), and tears down.

Async tests run on paused time (#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]), so the machines' 5-second polls and 30-second backoffs cost nothing. Database tests use Db::open_in_memory().

The launch-machine suite pins the behaviors that matter most:

  • capacity triggers compensation and moves to the next region; quota skips the whole region; unavailable skips without teardown
  • a transient create error after the request landed adopts the instance instead of creating a second one
  • a fatal error after create tears down before aborting
  • a failed teardown becomes LEAKED, and the next run cleans up first
  • a crash while Booting resumes without a second create
  • an unsupported feature is rejected even when a running VM could be reused, and the VM's record is left untouched

docs.title: CI
docs.text: Workflow Runs .github/workflows/unit.yml fmt, clippy (-D warnings), unit tests on Linux and macOS, MSRV (1.91.1) check .github/workflows/integration.yml vendor-stubs (every HTTP cloud adapter against its stub), aws-moto (AWS against the moto emulator, as a service container), and docker-e2e (the Docker e2e suite plus the acceptance-harness self-test, with GPUPROV_E2E_REQUIRE_DOCKER=1 so a missing daemon fails the job instead of skipping) .github/workflows/docs.yml strict MkDocs build on docs PRs; deploys to GitHub Pages on pushes to main

docs.title: Manual testing against real clouds
docs.text: Use GPUPROV_HOME=/tmp/gp to keep state away from ~/.gpu-provisioner, and RUST_LOG=debug for verbose progress. gpuprov status <name> shows the journaled transitions with failure details.

docs.title: Vendor API stubs
docs.text:
Every cloud adapter is tested at three levels:

Level What runs Catches unit / mock one adapter call against a canned wiremock response parsing and error classification of single calls vendor stubs (this page) the real adapter + launch/teardown state machines against a stateful simulation of the vendor's API cross-call bugs: an instance that never shows up in the list, a delete that leaves a volume behind, a retried create that duplicates, a boot script that never reaches the VM acceptance the real cloud with a real account everything the documentation doesn't tell you

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
tests/vendor_stubs.rs is the integration-test crate. Under tests/stubs/:

  • route.rs — a small stateful layer on wiremock: one simulated account per stub, with requests routed to Fn(&Request, &mut Account) -> Response.
  • harness.rs — the [VendorStub] trait and the scenarios, written once.
  • <vendor>.rs — one module per vendor. Each module doc has a table mapping every endpoint the adapter calls to the vendor's API reference page, with the behavior simulated. Response shapes follow the vendor's spec, not gpuprov's parser, so the stubs check the adapters independently.

The adapter is built through provider::build from an AppConfig whose base_url points at the stub, which is the same configuration path users take. SSH is the only other simulated piece: an accepting connector that records the endpoint it was asked to reach, so the login the vendor reports is still checked.

docs.title: Scenarios (every vendor)
docs.text:
Scenario Proves lifecycle plan → create → boot → ready, with the vendor-reported SSH user/port → down, and the simulated account holds no per-VM billable resources afterwards capacity failover the vendor's documented "no capacity" response on create → compensation → the next offer launches; the failed attempt created nothing interrupt cancel (Ctrl-C) while the instance boots → teardown → nothing left reuse provisioning the same name again adopts the running instance, with no second create boot script on clouds that run one, the boot script (body and env) reaches the vendor in its native form, and teardown removes every boot-script resource; other clouds skip it

The leak check has teeth. Breaking a stub so deletes trash Verda volumes instead of deleting them fails the lifecycle with billable resources left behind, and dropping Lambda's user_data fails the boot-script scenario.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Vendor Stub API reference the stub follows Faults simulated Documented assumptions RunPod runpod.rs REST v2 capacity (ErrorResponse), cursor pagination (page size 1) capacity status/body not documented Prime Intellect primeintellect.rs API reference capacity, offset pagination, DELETING → gone capacity body and delete transition not documented Verda verda.rs v1 API 503 service_unavailable capacity, OAuth token required, trashed vs permanent volume delete ip untyped in the spec Massed Compute massedcompute.rs API v1 "No Availability" launch error, unknown SSH key names, os_booted boot flag deploy-error status/body not documented; only rented status documented Hyperstack hyperstack.rs Infrahub API (OpenAPI) out_of_stock on create, duplicate environment/keypair (409) stock-out wording not documented; volumes/IPs not modelled separately Lambda lambda.rs Cloud API insufficient-capacity, ruleset in-use on delete, page_token pagination, plus a dedicated firewall-ruleset test — GCP gcp.rs Compute Engine REST v1 asynchronous ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED on the insert operation stockout HTTP code not documented AWS tests/aws_moto.rs EC2 API via the moto emulator — moto can't return capacity errors (failover not run) and boots instantly (interrupt runs during the SSH wait)

AWS uses moto, a maintained EC2/SSM emulator, rather than a hand-written stub: the EC2 Query/XML protocol is not worth re-implementing. The test seeds what moto lacks (an internet-gateway route; an explicit AMI, since moto refuses the public SSM AMI parameters) through moto's own API.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
cargo test --test vendor_stubs                 # all vendors (also part of `cargo test`)
cargo test --test vendor_stubs hyperstack      # one vendor

docker run -d --rm -p 127.0.0.1:5000:5000 motoserver/moto:5.2.3
GPUPROV_MOTO_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:5000 cargo test --test aws_moto -- --ignored

CI runs both in .github/workflows/integration.yml (jobs vendor-stubs and aws-moto, the latter with moto as a service container).

docs.title: Adding a stub for a new cloud
docs.text:
1. Create tests/stubs/<cloud>.rs and add mod <cloud>; to tests/stubs/mod.rs.
  2. Simulate the endpoints the adapter calls, following the vendor's reference, and document each one in the module's endpoint table with its doc link.
  3. Implement VendorStub: seed at least two in-stock offers, inject the vendor's real capacity error, model boot and delete transitions, count every per-VM billable resource in leftovers(), and record boot payloads if the cloud runs boot scripts.
  4. End the module with vendor_suite!(<Stub>);.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
Global flag: --config <PATH> selects the config file (default ~/.gpu-provisioner/config.toml; see Configuration).

Environment: GPUPROV_HOME relocates all local state, and RUST_LOG=debug gives verbose progress. Logs go to stderr and summaries to stdout.

docs.title: gpuprov provision
docs.text:
Provision a VM and block until it is SSH-ready and, unless k3s is turned off, until its cluster is validated. Re-running the command with the same --name is idempotent: a running VM is verified and reused, and an interrupted run is resumed.

Flag Meaning --name <NAME> VM name: lowercase letters, digits and -, up to 40 characters. It also works as name: in the spec file. --spec <FILE> YAML spec file. Flags override its fields. --cloud <ID> aws (default), gcp, massedcompute, hyperstack, lambda, verda, primeintellect, runpod, or docker. --instance-type <T> Exact type: g5.xlarge, g2-standard-8, hyperstack/n3-H100x1, "NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3" (RunPod), 1H100.80S.22V (Verda), gpu_1x_a6000 (Lambda), n3-RTX-A6000x1 (Hyperstack), or container. Cannot be combined with --gpus. --gpus <NAME[:N]> GPU shorthand resolved by the cloud's catalog, e.g. T4:1, L4:1, A100-80GB:8, H100:8. --region <R> Candidate region, in failover order. Repeatable. Region names are cloud-specific. --zone <Z> Pin to one zone (AWS and GCP) or data center (Prime Intellect, RunPod). --image <ID> (alias --ami) Machine-image override (container image on RunPod). --disk <GB> Root disk size (default 100). --spot Spot or preemptible capacity, where the cloud supports it. --port <P> Extra inbound port besides SSH. Repeatable. Requires a cloud with firewall control. --ssh-user <U> Login user to create (default ubuntu). Marketplace clouds dictate their own. --k8s Require the k3s cluster. It's on by default; this re-enables it when the config turns it off, and it fails on clouds that can't host k3s (guide). --no-k8s Plain VM: skip k3s. --retry-until-up When every offer fails, wait 30s and re-plan, forever.

Unsupported feature/cloud combinations, such as --port on Prime Intellect, are rejected before anything is planned.

Spec file example:

name: trainer
cloud: gcp
gpus: L4:1
regions: [us-central1, us-east1]
disk_gb: 200
kubernetes: false   # plain VM; omit to use the config default (on)

docs.title: gpuprov ssh <NAME> [-- CMD...]
docs.text: Opens an interactive shell, or runs one command and propagates its exit code. It uses the recorded user and port.

docs.title: gpuprov list
docs.text:
Lists every VM row: state, provider, region and zone, type, instance id, and endpoint (host:port when the port isn't 22).

States: PROVISIONING, UP, FAILED, TERMINATED, and LEAKED. LEAKED means teardown could not be confirmed. Run down again.

docs.title: gpuprov status <NAME>
docs.text: Shows the VM row, the last operation's state (marked in flight if it was interrupted), and up to 30 recent journaled transitions with failure details. This is the place to look when a provision fails.

docs.title: gpuprov down <NAME>
docs.text: Terminates the VM's instances, waits until they are gone, deletes per-VM side resources (security group or firewall rule), and removes local SSH and kubeconfig files. Ctrl-C does not stop a teardown halfway; press it twice to force-exit, then re-run to resume.

docs.title: gpuprov kubeconfig <NAME>
docs.text: For cluster VMs, re-runs the cluster steps (install check with SSH fallback, API wait, kubeconfig fetch, and validation) and rewrites ~/.gpu-provisioner/kube/<NAME>.yaml.

docs.title: gpuprov tunnel <NAME>
docs.text: For clusters on clouds without inbound-port control (Massed Compute, Verda, Prime Intellect), forwards 127.0.0.1:16443 to the node's API server. The kubeconfig of such clusters already points there. Keep it running while you use kubectl.

docs.title: Local state
docs.text:
Everything lives under ~/.gpu-provisioner, or under $GPUPROV_HOME when set:

~/.gpu-provisioner/
├── config.toml        # optional CLI config (below)
├── state.db           # SQLite: VM rows + state-machine journal
├── keys/              # the shared ed25519 keypair (generated on first use)
├── ssh/<name>         # per-VM ssh config, Include'd from ~/.ssh/config
├── sockets/           # ssh ControlMaster sockets
└── kube/<name>.yaml   # kubeconfigs of --k8s clusters (0600)

docs.title: config.toml
docs.text:
All sections are optional. Unknown keys are rejected.

[aws]
profile = "default"            # or explicit static credentials:
# access_key_id = "..."
# secret_access_key = "..."
# session_token = "..."        # optional

[gcp]
project = "my-project"         # else $GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT / gcloud config
# access_token = "..."         # else $GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN / gcloud auth print-access-token
regions = ["us-central1"]      # default failover order for --cloud gcp

[primeintellect]
api_key = "..."                # else $PRIME_API_KEY, else ~/.prime/config.json
# team_id = "..."              # bill pods to a team
# regions = ["united_states"]  # default region filter (empty = anywhere)

[runpod]
api_key = "..."                # else $RUNPOD_API_KEY, else ~/.runpod/config.toml
# regions = ["north_america"]  # continents or ISO country codes (empty = anywhere)
# image = "runpod/pytorch:..." # default: runpod/base with CUDA 12.9

[massedcompute]
api_key = "..."                # else $MASSED_COMPUTE_API_KEY

[hyperstack]
api_key = "..."                # else $HYPERSTACK_API_KEY
# regions = ["CANADA-1"]       # default: CANADA-1, US-1 (Norway only when asked)

[lambda]
api_key = "..."                # else $LAMBDA_API_KEY
# regions = ["us-east-1"]      # default: US regions

[verda]
client_id = "..."              # else $VERDA_CLIENT_ID
client_secret = "..."          # else $VERDA_CLIENT_SECRET
# regions = ["FIN-01"]         # location codes or ISO country codes (empty = anywhere)

[docker]
# image = "my/sshd:tag"        # default: built locally from an embedded Dockerfile

[defaults]
regions = ["us-west-2", "us-east-1"]   # AWS failover order when the spec has none
disk_gb = 100
ssh_user = "ubuntu"
kubernetes = true                      # every VM becomes a k3s node; false = plain VMs

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
For a launch, values come from CLI flags first, then the spec YAML, then the config file. That includes the k3s choice: --k8s/--no-k8s, then kubernetes: in the spec, then [defaults] kubernetes. Region names are cloud-specific, so each cloud has its own default region list. AWS uses [defaults] regions; the other clouds use their own section.

Whether an empty region list is allowed is the cloud's call. AWS and GCP require at least one region. Prime Intellect treats an empty list as "anywhere in the marketplace".

docs.title: Credentials by cloud
docs.text: Cloud Resolution order AWS static keys in [aws], then [aws] profile, then the default AWS chain (env vars, ~/.aws, IMDS) GCP [gcp] access_token, then $GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN, then gcloud auth print-access-token (cached, refreshed before expiry). Project: [gcp] project, then $GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT/$CLOUDSDK_CORE_PROJECT, then gcloud config get-value project Prime Intellect [primeintellect] api_key, then $PRIME_API_KEY, then the prime CLI's ~/.prime/config.json RunPod [runpod] api_key, then $RUNPOD_API_KEY, then the runpod CLI's ~/.runpod/config.toml Massed Compute [massedcompute] api_key, then $MASSED_COMPUTE_API_KEY (create at vm.massedcompute.com → Settings → API) Hyperstack [hyperstack] api_key, then $HYPERSTACK_API_KEY Lambda [lambda] api_key, then $LAMBDA_API_KEY Verda [verda] client_id/client_secret, then $VERDA_CLIENT_ID/$VERDA_CLIENT_SECRET (exchanged for an OAuth token, refreshed automatically) Docker the local Docker daemon (docker info must work)

docs.title: Kubernetes (k3s)
docs.text:
Every VM becomes a single-node k3s cluster by default: real Kubernetes, managed by systemd on the node. You deploy apps with plain kubectl. There is no custom controller; k3s itself is the reconciler.

gpuprov provision --name gpu-k8s --gpus L4:1 --cloud gcp --region us-central1
export KUBECONFIG=~/.gpu-provisioner/kube/gpu-k8s.yaml
kubectl get nodes
kubectl apply -f examples/gpu-test.yaml    # runs nvidia-smi in a pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu
kubectl logs job/gpu-test

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text:
Scope How one VM gpuprov provision --no-k8s ..., or kubernetes: false in the spec file everywhere [defaults] kubernetes = false in config.toml (then --k8s opts a VM back in)

On clouds that cannot host k3s (the Docker test cloud), the default is skipped with a note. An explicit --k8s there is rejected before anything is created.

docs.title: How it gets installed
docs.text:
The cluster is a state machine layered on the VM launch machine. The installer can reach the node by two routes:

  1. Boot. On clouds that can run a script at first boot, the installer runs while the VM boots, so the install overlaps the wait for SSH. AWS, GCP, Hyperstack and Lambda get it through cloud-init user data; Verda gets it as a startup script.

  2. SSH. Once the VM is up, gpuprov checks what the boot run did (one SSH round trip: a status marker, cloud-init status, the k3s unit, GPU presence):

    Found Action installed at boot, k3s running skip straight to the API check boot install still running wait (up to 15 minutes) boot install failed, never ran (no cloud-init, reused VM), or still running after 15 min push the installer over SSH a GPU the boot run didn't see push the installer over SSH to add the GPU runtime

The two routes never race. The installer takes a host-wide lock, so an SSH run waits for a boot run still holding it. The installer is also idempotent: it writes /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml itself and restarts k3s only when that file changes.

What the installer does: if nvidia-smi works, it installs nvidia-container-toolkit (unless the image already has it), makes nvidia the default containerd runtime, and applies the NVIDIA device plugin (pinned v0.19.3). Then it installs k3s.

After installing, gpuprov:

  1. waits for the API (/readyz, up to 10 minutes);
  2. writes the kubeconfig: it reads /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml, renames the cluster/user/context to gpuprov-<name>, points server at the access endpoint, and saves it with mode 0600;
  3. validates on the node that the node is Ready, CoreDNS is ready, and (with a GPU) nvidia.com/gpu is allocatable. In direct mode it also checks that the API certificate covers the public host and that the API port is reachable from your machine. That last check catches firewall problems that on-node checks can't see.

If a cluster step fails, the VM is kept so you can debug it with gpuprov ssh (the boot log is /var/log/cloud-init-output.log). Re-run the same provision command to retry; it reuses the VM and re-checks the install. Or run gpuprov down to remove it.

docs.title: Access modes
docs.text:
Mode When Kubeconfig server You run Direct the cloud can open ports (AWS, GCP, Hyperstack, Lambda) https://<public-ip>:6443 nothing SSH tunnel the cloud can't (Massed Compute, Verda, Prime Intellect) https://127.0.0.1:16443 gpuprov tunnel <name> in another terminal

The API certificate covers the public host and always covers 127.0.0.1. At boot the installer learns the public IP from the cloud's metadata service. If it can't, validation notices that the certificate doesn't cover the host and re-runs the installer once with it.

Direct mode exposure

In direct mode, ports 6443, 80, and 443 are open to 0.0.0.0/0, now on every VM by default. API access is gated by the client certificate inside the kubeconfig, so treat that file as a secret, or use --no-k8s for VMs that don't need a cluster.
